title: Opponent spits at the car window in rage; he says this proves he's happier
dek: His 'happier person's yield': before conflict, determine who's happier, and that person backs down. This logic reframes not fighting back as rational—not fearful.
why: Improvised comedy with stand-up comedians sparring—low on substantive content, but real anecdotes about road rage and drunk driving are more interesting than the debates.
who: Listeners who enjoy watching stand-up comedians riff with bad logic and jokes, or are curious about Luo Yonghao's own road rage and dispute stories. Not for people seeking substance.
skip: The mid-section debate about whether performers should work all-night script revisions is low on information and can be skipped.

points.h: Emotional stability is not a virtue—it's social conditioning
points.body: Society never questions whether adults should be emotionally passionate, yet uniquely demands they be stable—a standard that only tightens with age. This is not a virtue but a rule imposed without justification.

points.h: Stupidity is worse to endure than malice
points.body: Malice used to seem worse than incompetence. Now incompetence hurts more: you can rightfully attack a bad actor, but a well-meaning fool offers no clean response. Criticize and you seem cruel; stay silent and you choke.

points.h: Blocking and deleting are addictive thrills
points.body: Blocking and deleting feed addiction. The practice calcifies into a reflex until the person cannot tolerate disagreement. Two methods emerge: mock sarcastically to disguise attacks as jokes, or block ruthlessly. Both become compulsive; both harden into arrogance.

points.h: Never block: actively search your own name to hear criticism
points.body: Almost never block anyone; actively search your own name to find criticism. The habit—like dumpster-diving after meals—prevents you from becoming insular. Only accept affirmation, and you narrow into yourself.

points.h: Rant for hours and watch every curse word become meows
points.body: During one rare late-night argument, he expected his opponent to suffer sleeplessly. But next morning, his hundreds of curses had been auto-replaced with meows (喵喵喵) by the platform's profanity filter. His rage became wordplay; furious, he left a scathing App Store review of the app itself.

points.h: Refusing to fight back proves you're the happier person
points.body: During a road-rage confrontation, the other driver threatened him; Luo stayed in his car filming. When the man spat on the window in frustration before leaving, Luo invented a rule: before any conflict, determine who is happier, and the happier person yields. By this logic, remaining calm while your opponent loses control proves you're happier—so not fighting back is rational, not fear.

points.h: The drunk driver's mother flips on a dime
points.body: In an alcohol-fueled collision, the at-fault driver's mother arrived in tears begging mercy; Luo was prepared to settle. But when she spotted his car's temporary license plate, she flipped instantly and counter-attacked: wasn't he driving illegally? This prompted his sole profane outburst at a woman.

points.h: To broaden your mind, you must engage with people you despise
points.body: Actively engage with people whose values repel you. Everyone believes they're doing good—no one thinks they're the villain. Understanding why someone acts the way they do reveals your own blind spots. Retreat into agreement-only circles and you harden into something smaller.

terms.def: Society's unreasonable moral demands imposed on a person; in this episode, the demand that adults be emotionally stable. Likely a misspelling of PUA.

quotes.text: We tell young people how to be people. But the moment you become an adult, we immediately say: be stable. That's society's POA on adults.
If you know someone is a bad person, you can attack him, curse him—no problem. But if he's stupid and means well but ends up causing harm—what do you do?
These two methods may not work for you, but they work for me. The first one: since he's stupid, you can't curse him out directly, so you use a joking, sarcastic tone.
Because if people only interact with those who affirm them, they become increasingly arrogant and narrow-minded.
When I block someone, in my mind I'm executing him. I take this big blade, I chop his head clean off—that's what it feels like.
The happier person's yield principle: before anyone yields, first determine who's happier between us, then the happier person chooses to yield.
Because no one thinks they're a bad person—in everything they do, they believe they're good. Why do they see themselves that way?—that's what I'm really curious about.
